---
title: "Reference · Understanding ResScan's output"
subtitle: "The files, the columns, the metric names — and the one label that trips everyone up: multiple."
---

You've run ResScan. Now let's read what it produced — the files, the columns, the
metric names, and one word that trips everyone up: **`multiple`**. Keep this page open
in a tab; it's a lookup, not a lesson.

## What a run produces

A single `resscan` run makes one folder named after your `-o` prefix. Batch mode
makes one such folder *per sample*. Inside:

| File / folder | What it is |
|---|---|
| `<prefix>_homscan.tsv` | **The main table.** One row per detected AMR *gene* (homology models — whole-gene presence). All metrics as columns. |
| `<prefix>_homscan_detailed.tsv` | The same, but one row **per read-to-gene hit** — the raw evidence behind the summary. |
| `<prefix>_varscan.tsv` | AMR from **point mutations** — one row per resistance-conferring variant detected. |
| `<prefix>_homscan_html/` | Interactive per-gene **coverage plots** (open in a browser) — see *where* along each gene reads landed. |
| `<prefix>_varscan_html/` | The same, for the variant hits. |
| `logs/`, `tmp/` | Run logs and intermediates — safe to ignore (or delete). |

The two `.tsv` files are what you analyse. The HTML plots are how you *sanity-check* a
hit — a real gene shows reads spread along its length, not piled on one spot.

## HomScan vs VarScan — both are genes

This distinction confuses people, so plainly: **both tables report genes.** The
difference is *how resistance is detected*.

| | **HomScan** (`_homscan.tsv`) | **VarScan** (`_varscan.tsv`) |
|---|---|---|
| Detects resistance by… | **presence** of a whole resistance gene (homology) | a **specific point mutation** in an otherwise-normal gene |
| CARD model | homolog model | protein-variant & rRNA-variant models |
| Typical example | KPC, TEM β-lactamases (the gene *is* the resistance) | `gyrA` S83L, 16S rRNA mutations (the *mutation* is the resistance) |

So a fluoroquinolone-resistant *E. coli* carries a normal-looking `gyrA` gene — only a
single base tells you it's resistant. That's VarScan's job; HomScan would just see "a
`gyrA`." You want both.

### Anatomy of an ARO id

Every row is keyed by a CARD **ARO** (Antibiotic Resistance Ontology) id. ResScan
formats it so you can read it at a glance:

```default
ARO_3002530__AAC_3_-Ib__H
ARO_3003411__Ecol_16S_TET__R__a964g
└──┬─────┘   └───┬────┘  │   └─┬─┘
 accession     gene name  │   mutation (a→g at position 964)
                          └─ model code
```

**Model code** — the trailing letter: `H` homolog · `V` protein variant · `R` rRNA
variant · `O` overexpression · `K` knockout. `H` rows live in HomScan; the
mutation-based codes drive VarScan.

## The columns

Both `.tsv` files share the same five annotation columns, then the metrics:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `AMR_Gene_Family` | The CARD family the gene belongs to (e.g. `KPC beta-lactamase`). |
| `ARO` | The ARO id (see above). |
| `ARO_Name` | Human-readable gene / variant name. |
| `Drug_Class` | Antibiotic class(es) affected — `;`-separated if several. |
| `Resistance_Mechanism` | How it works (e.g. `antibiotic inactivation`). |
| *metrics…* | One column per abundance metric (next section). |

## The metrics — read the name, know the number

There are fifteen metric columns, but you don't memorise them — you **decode** them.
Every name is built from three parts:

```default
 [ R | F ]  PK  [ '' | G | M | PC | PMC | PGC ]
   │        │      └─ what you divide by (the denominator)
   │        └─ Per Kilobase of gene length (always)
   └─ counting Reads or Fragments
```

**Part 1 — Reads or Fragments.** `R…` counts reads; `F…` counts **fragments** (a
read *pair* = one DNA fragment). ResScan computes both families for every gene; the
**read-based** metrics are the default — the per-cell `RPKPMC` below is the
recommended headline number.

**Part 2 — `PK`.** Every metric divides by gene length in kb, so a long gene and a
short gene are comparable.

**Part 3 — the denominator** — this is the one that matters:

| Suffix | Divides by… | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| *(none)* — `RPK`/`FPK` | nothing else | raw length-normalised count |
| `G` — `RPKG`/`FPKG` | total **gigabases** sequenced | abundance per unit of data |
| `M` — `RPKM`/`FPKM` | total **millions of reads/fragments** | the classic metagenomics unit |
| `PC` — `RPKPC`/`FPKPC` | **per bacterial cell** (via single-copy genes) | copies per cell |
| `PMC` — **`RPKPMC`**/`FPKPMC` | per **million** cells | copies per cell, scaled ×10⁶ |
| `PGC` — `RPKPGC`/`FPKPGC` | per **billion** cells | copies per cell, scaled ×10⁹ |

Plus two standalone columns: `Read_Count` / `Fragment_Count` (the raw tallies) and
`Lateral_Coverage_%` (how much of the gene's length was actually covered — your
best single guard against a spurious hit).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Which one should I use? `RPKPMC`
`RPKPMC` is ResScan's **preferred default metric**: read-based, length-normalised, and
scaled **per bacterial cell** against universal single-copy genes — so it's comparable
across samples of different depth *and* not thrown off by inflation from non-bacterial
(e.g. human) reads. The `M` scaling just turns tiny per-cell fractions into readable
numbers. This is the metric the [analysis page](analysis.qmd) uses, and the reason
[host removal](vanish.qmd) is safe rather than sacred. ResScan still reports the full
family of metrics above for anyone who needs them — a fuller account of why RPKPMC
makes the best default is the subject of a separate, forthcoming paper.
:::

## The word `multiple`

Short reads sometimes can't be pinned to a *single* gene — a fragment matches several
CARD alleles equally well. ResScan refuses to guess, and labels it **`multiple`**
rather than arbitrarily crediting one gene. You'll see it two ways:

- **In the `ARO` column: `multiple[…]`** — the read hit several alleles, and the
  bracket lists exactly which ones (`family;ARO` pairs, `|`-separated). Fully
  transparent: you can see the candidates.
- **In the `AMR_Gene_Family` column: `multiple`** — used only when even the *family*
  can't be agreed on. If most of the tied alleles belong to one family (above a
  consensus threshold), ResScan keeps that family name and only the `ARO` stays
  `multiple[…]`; if they're spread across families, the family itself becomes
  `multiple`.

Its metrics are still computed honestly (gene length is averaged over the tied
alleles). Practically: a `multiple` row is **real resistance you can trust at the
family level** (often even the specific family), just not resolved to one exact
allele — usually a limit of read length, not of the tool.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Don't drop `multiple` rows
They're genuine hits. In the sink data, `multiple` is one of the more abundant
"families" precisely because closely related β-lactamase alleles are hard to tell
apart from short reads — discarding it would throw away real signal.
:::

## Batch mode: the aggregated tables

`resscan_aggregate` takes all those per-sample `_homscan.tsv` / `_varscan.tsv` files
and pivots them into **one file per metric**, with the five annotation columns then
one column per sample:

```default
SR_homscan_RPKPMC.tsv               SR_varscan_RPKPMC.tsv
SR_homscan_Lateral_Coverage_%.tsv   … (one per metric, ×2 for hom/var)
```

That's the shape the [analysis](analysis.qmd) reads: pick the file for the metric
you want (`RPKPMC` by default), and every sample is already a column.
